1163.title: Ananda and Rahula (Kern ch. 9)
1163.hook: the attendant and the son receive their promises too
1163.howItsDone: Buddhist communities remember Ananda as the attendant who heard and kept the Buddha's teaching, and Rahula as his son who became a monk; in the Lotus Sutra both receive the promise of future buddhahood in chapter nine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man lived poor for years with a priceless jewel sewn into his coat, until a friend said look. Your line: the jewel in the coat.

Stay for the end of a film's credits. Far down, in small type, is the person who held the umbrella between takes, the one who drove the actors at five in the morning. Somebody decided they belonged on the screen too. Chapter nine of the Lotus Sutra is that part of the credits. Promises of future awakening have gone out to the great disciples, chapter after chapter. Two people close to the Buddha have stood nearby the whole time: the man who walked beside him every day, and the boy who was his son. You met them both in year one.
screen: `THE NAMES AT THE END OF THE CREDITS.` → `PROMISES GOING OUT.` → `TWO WHO STOOD CLOSEST.`

segments.voice: First, they ask. Ananda and Rahula think, what about us? They bow at the Buddha's feet and say it plainly: we have a claim here too. One of us attends you and keeps your teaching; the other is your son. Name us, and our wish is fulfilled. Behind them a whole crowd of monks, some still in training and some finished, stand up too. Second, Ananda. The Buddha answers with a story. Long ago, under a Buddha of a past age, he and Ananda set their minds on awakening together. Ananda gave himself to hearing much; the Buddha gave himself to effort. So one woke first, and the other became the keeper of everything he heard. Neither road is left out. Ananda will be a Buddha too, and hearing this, he remembers his own old vow. Third, Rahula. He will be the eldest son of future Buddhas, as he is the Buddha's son now. Then a tender line, in paraphrase: Rahula's quiet practice, nobody knows it but me. The one always introduced as somebody's son has a practice of his own, and his father has been watching. Fourth, why it matters. Being close to someone great can feel like living in their shadow: the assistant, the sibling, the spouse, the famous one's kid, thanked in passing if at all. Chapter nine stops and gives each a future with their own name and story. Then it turns to the crowd behind them and gives them promises too.

1164.title: The preacher (Kern ch. 10)
1164.hook: whoever keeps even one verse of this sutra is to be honored
1164.tomorrow: The stupa in the sky (Kern ch. 11)
1164.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that treasure the Lotus Sutra, people keep, recite, copy and explain the sutra, and the one who teaches it is honored; chapter ten is where the sutra itself praises that work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the attendant and the son stood up and asked, and each got a promise of his own. Your line: them too.

A grandmother knows one proverb and says it at exactly the right moment, every time. Is she a teacher? How much of a teaching do you have to carry before you count as carrying it? The whole book? A degree? A robe and a title? Chapter ten of the Lotus Sutra answers, and its answer is smaller than the question. The Buddha turns to a bodhisattva named Bhaishajyaraja, the Medicine King, and talks about the figure the chapter is named for. Not a great disciple, not a Buddha. Just someone who passes the words along.
screen: `HOW MUCH DO YOU HAVE TO CARRY?` → `ONE PROVERB, RIGHT ON TIME.` → `THE ONE WHO PASSES IT ALONG.`

segments.voice: First, the size of it. Whoever hears even a single verse of this sutra, the Buddha says, and is glad of it for one moment, he foretells their awakening. Whoever keeps it, reads it, explains it or copies it, even one verse, and honors the book with flowers and incense, is to be honored as if they were the Tathagata himself. Second, the messenger. Whoever explains this teaching to even one person, even quietly, in private, is a messenger the Tathagata has sent. One listener is enough. Third, a picture. A man in dry country digs for water. The sand comes up dry, and he keeps digging. Then the earth turns damp, then muddy, and he knows water is close. Hearing this teaching, the Buddha says, is that damp earth: a sign that awakening is near. Fourth, how to do it. The chapter gives the preacher a room, a robe and a seat. The room is compassion for all beings. The robe is patience, gentleness under pressure. The seat is seeing that all things are empty. Enter the room, put on the robe, sit on the seat, and then speak. So the preacher isn't the loudest voice. It's anyone who carries one verse, kindly and patiently, to one other person. The bar is low. The honor is high.

1165.title: The stupa in the sky (Kern ch. 11)
1165.hook: a jeweled stupa rises from the earth; an ancient Buddha inside invites the Buddha to share his seat
1165.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the scene of Many Jewels and Shakyamuni seated together in the stupa is recited and pictured in temple art, and the two Buddhas side by side are honored together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the preacher: anyone who carries this teaching to even one person, honored as a messenger. Your line: even one verse.

The ground opens in the middle of the sermon. Up out of the earth rises a stupa, a tower built to hold the remains of a holy one, and this one is made of jewels. It climbs, and hangs in the sky, hung with banners and bells, giving off fragrance. Then a voice comes out of it, praising the Buddha for teaching the Lotus. The whole assembly stares up at a reliquary that speaks. Chapter eleven has begun, and it only gets stranger.
screen: `THE GROUND OPENS.` → `A JEWELED TOWER RISES.` → `A VOICE FROM INSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the tower. A bodhisattva named Mahapratibhana asks: what is this? Inside, the Buddha explains, is the whole body of a Buddha named Prabhutaratna, Many Jewels, from a world long past, who entered final nirvana ages ago. Second, why he came. While still on the path, Many Jewels vowed: wherever this sutra is taught, in any world, my stupa will rise out of the ground to hear it, and to say, well done. So a Buddha of the far past has come as a listener, and as a witness. Third, the door. The assembly wants to see him, but the stupa won't open until the Buddha calls home every form of himself teaching across the worlds in every direction. They arrive, and the worlds are made clean to hold them. Then the Buddha rises into the air and opens the door with a finger, and the text says it sounds like a great bolt sliding back on a city gate. Inside, Many Jewels sits whole, as if deep in meditation. Fourth, the seat. Many Jewels moves over and offers half his seat, and the Buddha sits down beside him. Two Buddhas, one from ages ago and one from now, side by side in a jeweled tower in the sky. Then the Buddha lifts the whole assembly into the air to be near them. Some readers hear in the seat a picture of the teaching itself: not owned by one age, shared across them. The sutra simply shows it. One seat, two Buddhas, room enough.

1166.title: The dragon king's daughter (Kern ch. 11)
1166.hook: in this chapter the young naga princess offers a jewel and awakens in an instant, to the disciples' surprise
1166.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the naga king's daughter is remembered as the girl who awakened in an instant, and traditions read the change of her body in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a jeweled tower hung in the sky, and an ancient Buddha moved over to make room. Your line: two on one seat.

Someone in the middle of chapter eleven says, out loud, that he doesn't believe it. Not a scoffer in the back row: a bodhisattva named Prajnakuta, attendant to the Buddha of the jeweled tower. He's just been told that a young girl, daughter of the dragon king who rules under the sea, has reached the very edge of awakening. He knows the road is supposed to take ages, lifetimes, countless gifts and sacrifices. A child, from the ocean, from a family of serpents? No. Then she walks in.
screen: `HE DOESN'T BELIEVE IT.` → `A GIRL FROM UNDER THE SEA.` → `THEN SHE WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. The bodhisattva Manjushri rises out of the ocean, where he's been teaching the Lotus in the palace of Sagara, the naga king. Nagas are serpent beings of the waters; English often calls them dragons. Has anyone there taken this teaching in deeply enough to awaken quickly? Prajnakuta asks. Yes, says Manjushri: Sagara's young daughter, wise, kind, steady in meditation. Second, the doubt. The Buddha himself strove for ages, Prajnakuta says; he can't believe a girl could do it in a moment. Then the girl appears, bows, and praises the Buddha. And the senior disciple Sariputra adds his own objection: a woman's body, he says, cannot reach buddhahood. Third, the jewel. She offers the Buddha a jewel of enormous worth, and he accepts it at once. She turns to the two doubters: was that quick? Very quick, they say. Watch me, she says, awaken faster than that. Fourth, the instant. Before the whole assembly, the text shows her form changing to a male one, and she appears in a world to the south, seated under a bodhi tree, fully awake, teaching. Prajnakuta and Sariputra go silent. That change of body is read in more than one way. Some readers hear the old assumption that a woman must first become a man. Others point out that she awakens anyway, faster than the objection can finish, and hear the objection answered. The chapter ends with two senior figures silent, and a young girl teaching.

1167.title: Exertion (Kern ch. 12)
1167.hook: the bodhisattvas vow to teach the sutra in hard times; Mahapajapati and Yasodhara are given promises
1167.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that keep the Lotus Sutra, the bodhisattvas' vow in this chapter is recited as a model of patient effort, and Mahaprajapati and Yasodhara are remembered as receiving their own promise of buddhahood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a young girl from under the sea offered a jewel and awakened while two senior figures doubted her. Your line: in an instant.

Here's a promise with a warning label. A crowd of bodhisattvas tells the Buddha: after you're gone, we'll keep teaching this sutra. Then, in the same breath, they describe how bad it will be. People will be proud and hard to reach. They'll insult us, threaten us, throw some of us out. We'll keep going anyway. It's a vow made with eyes open, after reading the forecast. And tucked into the same chapter, two women who have been watching get a promise of their own. You met them both in year one.
screen: `A PROMISE WITH A WARNING LABEL.` → `IT WILL BE BAD.` → `WE'LL KEEP GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the vow. Two bodhisattvas, Bhaishajyaraja, the Medicine King, and Mahapratibhana, with their companions, promise to keep and teach this sutra after the Buddha's death, in an age when people will be hard to train. Monks who've already received promises vow to teach it in other worlds. Second, Mahaprajapati, called Mahapajapati in Pali: the Buddha's aunt, standing with a great company of nuns, gazing at him. He notices the look and asks, in paraphrase: why look at me so sadly? Are you thinking I haven't named you? Then he names her. She too will become a Buddha, and the nuns with her. Third, Yasodhara, the mother of Rahula. She thinks: he still hasn't mentioned my name. And he does: her own future buddhahood, spoken before everyone. Both women are glad, and both vow to teach the sutra too. Fourth, the hard part. The Buddha looks at the bodhisattvas in silence, and they understand what he's asking. They answer in verse. In the fearful time to come, people will abuse us, threaten us with sticks and swords, and call us heretics. Some of the proud ones wearing robes will mock us and drive us out. We'll bear it. We don't cling to body or life; we care for the path. That's exertion here: not a burst of energy on a good morning, but the decision to keep going when the conditions are named and they're bad. And in the middle of it, the women watching from the side are seen, and named.

1168.title: The peaceful life (Kern ch. 13)
1168.hook: four ways to teach calmly; the jewel in the king's topknot
1168.tomorrow: From the cracks of the earth (Kern ch. 14)
1168.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, this chapter's guidance on teaching gently, without quarreling or speaking ill of others, is studied as a model for how to share the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bodhisattvas vowed to keep teaching through insults and threats, and two women were seen and named. Your line: in hard times.

What's the calmest way to say the thing you think matters most? Picture teaching something you love to people who insult you for it. Do you shout back? Win the argument? In chapter thirteen, Manjushri asks the Buddha exactly that: in the hard age to come, how should a bodhisattva teach this sutra? The answer isn't a strategy for winning. It's a way of living so steady that the teaching can be heard through it. Kern's English calls the chapter the peaceful life. And at the end, there's a king with one jewel he holds back.
screen: `TEACH HOW?` → `MANJUSHRI ASKS.` → `A KING WITH ONE JEWEL.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Manjushri asks how a bodhisattva can teach the sutra at peace when times are bad, and the Buddha answers with four things to keep. Second, body and tongue. Be patient and gentle, not rash, not easily rattled. Don't chase the powerful to win favor. Keep a quiet place to sit and see things as empty, without clinging. When you speak, don't dwell on the faults of other people, other teachers or other texts, and don't name people to praise them or tear them down. Answer kindly and plainly, in a way that fits the person asking. Third, the mind. No envy, flattery or deceit. Don't sneer at people still learning, and don't pick quarrels. Feel compassion for everyone. See the Buddhas as fathers and the bodhisattvas as teachers. And keep one wish alive: that people who haven't heard this teaching will someday be brought to it. Fourth, the jewel. A great king wins a war and rewards his soldiers: fields, villages, towns, clothes, gold, jewels, elephants, horses. But one thing he won't hand out, the jewel in the knot of his hair. Giving it lightly would astonish people. He keeps it for the one soldier whose deed is beyond all the rest. This sutra, the Buddha says, is that jewel. For a long time he gave other teachings; only now does he take this one out. So the peaceful life is how you carry the jewel: gently, without a fight, without belittling anyone, because what you carry is that precious.

1169.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the bodhisattvas who rise from the earth are honored as the ones entrusted with the sutra in this world, and some schools, including Nichiren Buddhism, give them and their leader a central place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four ways to teach calmly, and a king who kept one jewel in his hair for the deed beyond all others. Your line: the jewel in the topknot.

In spring, a crack in the sidewalk fills with green. Nobody planted it or watered it. It was down there all along, working in the dark, and one day it's just up. Chapter fourteen of the Lotus Sutra opens with an offer of help. Bodhisattvas from other worlds say to the Buddha: let us protect this sutra here after you're gone. A generous offer, and a sensible one. The Buddha turns it down. No need, he says. This world already has its own. Then the ground starts to split.

segments.voice: First, the refusal. The visitors mean well, but this world has bodhisattvas of its own who will keep the sutra after him. Second, the earth opens. All across this world the ground cracks, and up rise bodhisattvas beyond counting, bodies shining gold, each with a great company of followers. They go up to the jeweled stupa still hanging in the sky and bow to the two Buddhas seated there. Four lead them, and all four names speak of conduct: superior, boundless, pure, and firm. Third, nobody knows them. Maitreya, who is said to be the next Buddha, has never seen a single one, and neither has anyone else. Who are these? The Buddha answers: I taught them, all of them, here in this world since my awakening. They've lived below, studying quietly, away from crowds. Fourth, the puzzle. Maitreya is honest about how strange that sounds. You awakened not long ago; how could you have taught so many? It's like a young man with dark hair pointing at white-haired elders and saying, these are my sons, while they nod and say, he's our father. Who would believe it? The chapter ends with that question in the air, and tomorrow answers it. This is the week's last day, so lay its chapters side by side: the attendant and the son, the one who teaches a single verse, a girl from under the sea, two women waiting to be named, and now a crowd nobody knew was there. All week, the Lotus kept counting the people nobody was counting.
